packets.key_finding: A nudge that shrouds the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cuts minimum-only payers by 23% at six months but does not significantly reduce debt, and it lowers autopay enrollment overall, increasing missed payments.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts, six-month follow-up on payment behavior and autopay enrollment.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly tests the brief's central worry: a choice-architecture change can move a nominal enrollment/behavior metric while leaving the real outcome (amount paid down / saved) unchanged, and can have side effects (missed payments) among liquidity-constrained users — exactly the disengagement/harm pattern the support team is worried about for round-up savings.
limitations: credit-card debt paydown, not a savings product
US context, not EU
does not test opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment directly, only a shrouding nudge within autopay settings
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer financial self-directed setting showing a default-like nudge changes nominal behavior without changing the real outcome, contradicting the 'defaults always help' premise.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting at least 15 months and differing by rollout scope.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered EU DMA choice-screen rollout across iOS and Android.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest recent, EU-regulatory-context evidence that a mandated active-choice screen produces large, durable shifts away from a preset default, directly informing whether active choice can substitute for opt-out in the Entry decision.
limitations: studies browser choice, not a financial product
effect size may depend on rollout mechanics (new vs. existing devices) that may not transfer
packets.relevance_reason: Best available EU, at-scale, persistence-tracked comparison of active choice against defaults, central to the Entry decision.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, steady-state saving rates rise by only 0.6 percentage points from automatic enrollment and 0.3 points from default auto-escalation once job turnover, withdrawal on separation, and opt-outs from escalation are accounted for; only 40% of those defaulted into auto-escalation actually escalate on the first date.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal administrative-data analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out dynamics.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: default-driven enrollment gains shrink substantially once medium/long-run dynamics (withdrawal, opt-out, turnover) are modeled — directly bears on whether an opt-out round-up default would be vanity enrollment.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated turnover/vesting dynamics don't map onto a banking app
no EU or fintech context
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that default enrollment reliably lifts real savings once realistic attrition dynamics are modeled.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a 4,207-person five-European-country sample, default nudges shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (especially one people refuse) lowers ratings of the advisor's advice, an effect also of medium-to-large size, mediated by perceived honesty.
packets.methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, manipulating default presence and framing in investment/risk allocation decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the reputational/manipulation risk the brief flags: a default that shifts behavior can simultaneously erode trust in the institution presenting it, which should shape how the round-up default and any pre-selected multiplier are framed and communicated in the EU app.
limitations: wealth-manager advisory context rather than a self-serve banking app
risk-taking/investment allocation, not a round-up savings mechanism
does not report persistence beyond the immediate experimental session
packets.relevance_reason: EU multi-country experimental evidence on when a default reads as helpful vs manipulative, directly informing the dark-pattern risk the brief cares about.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and theoretical framework for downstream (long-run) default effects, showing they depend on the time course of choice/consumption, prior preferences, and salience of trade-offs, and sets a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent findings.
packets.methodology: Conceptual synthesis and framework paper drawing on the consumer-behavior default literature. Abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a structured lens for exactly the persistence question the brief asks — which conditions make a default's effect last vs fade — and should shape what the team measures at 6-12 months rather than just enrollment at day one.
limitations: theoretical/conceptual rather than a specific quantitative effect size
not focused on financial products specifically
no primary data of its own
packets.relevance_reason: A 2025 consumer-behavior framework directly organizing the downstream-persistence question central to the enrolment-design decision.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: At-scale field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide, though alerts captured less than half of potential avoidable savings.
packets.methodology: Large-scale field experiments at major UK banks measuring downstream financial outcomes of an auto-enrolled consumer banking feature.
packets.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that auto-enrollment into a passive banking-app feature can produce real, measurable financial benefit at scale, closely analogous to auto-enrolling users into round-up savings, while showing defaults capture only partial potential benefit.
limitations: measures overdraft alerts, not a savings-level enrolment decision
no comparison of opt-in vs opt-out vs active-choice enrolment designs
packets.relevance_reason: Closest real-world UK consumer-banking-app auto-enrolment evidence, directly analogous to the round-up feature's Entry decision.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: In 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost together (removing either alone collapses adherence), and adding an intermediate preset option (15% alongside 20/25/30%) captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6 million transaction records, validated against an independent stated-preference survey of tipping preferences, with counterfactual menu simulations.
packets.why_it_matters: The structural decomposition of why people accept preset menu options and the counterfactual analysis of adding an intermediate preset level transfers directly to the multiplier decision: it gives a method for testing whether adding a 2x-style intermediate option between 1x and 5x would capture most of the achievable benefit without the extremes.
limitations: tipping decisions, not savings or financial contributions
US taxi context, not EU or banking
welfare/counterfactual framework assumes a stated-preference benchmark that a savings-pot analogue would need to replicate
packets.relevance_reason: Explicit structural-modeling and counterfactual-menu-design method that transfers to deciding whether and where to pre-set the round-up multiplier.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, financial nudges framed around savings and targeting deliberate (System 2) decision-making were rated most favourably, with transparency having no significant effect on approval or perceived manipulation.
packets.methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment; 36 hypothetical financial intervention scenarios; representative sample of 2,100 Australians; six dependent variables including approval and manipulation.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern reputational risk named in the brief: shows how framing (savings vs spending) and messenger (bank) affect whether a nudge is perceived as helpful or manipulative, which should shape the messaging around whichever entry design is chosen.
limitations: Hypothetical vignettes rather than actual enrolment behaviour
Australian sample, not the EU regulatory context named in the brief
No measurement of enrolment, persistence, or amount saved
packets.relevance_reason: Tests perceived manipulation and approval of financial nudges, which is the dark-pattern risk criterion the brief explicitly flags.
packets.title: Do people like financial nudges?
packets.abstract: Abstract Do people like financial nudges? To answer that question we conducted a pre-registered survey presenting people with 36 hypothetical scenarios describing financial interventions. We varied levels of transparency (i.e., explaining how the interventions worked), framing (interventions framed in terms of spending, or saving), and ‘System’ (interventions could target either System 1 or System 2). Participants were a random sample of 2,100 people drawn from a representative Australian population. All financial interventions were tested across six dependent variables: approval, benefit, ethics, manipulation, the likelihood of use, as well as the likelihood of use if the intervention were to be proposed by a bank. Results indicate that people generally approve of financial interventions, rating them as neutral to positive across all dependent variables (except for manipulation, which was reverse coded). We find effects of framing and System. People have strong and significant preferences for System 2 interventions, and interventions framed in terms of savings. Transparency was not found to have a significant impact on how people rate financial interventions. Financial interventions continue to be rated positive, regardless of the messenger. Looking at demographics, we find that participants who were female, younger, living in metro areas and earning higher incomes were most likely to favor financial interventions, and this effect is especially strong for those aged under 45. We discuss the implications for these results as applied to the financial sector.

packets.key_finding: A synthesis of household finance evidence showing that choice-architecture interventions, including defaults and product design, systematically shift financial behaviour across savings, borrowing, payments, and insurance, alongside the underlying behavioural mechanisms.
packets.methodology: Narrative review/NBER chapter synthesizing empirical regularities and intervention evidence across household financial decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Serves as the review-of-effect-sizes the brief asks for: covers defaults and choice architecture across a wider range of self-directed consumer financial decisions than employer retirement plans alone, giving a broader base to calibrate expected default effect sizes for the round-up feature.
limitations: Narrative synthesis, not a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
abstract-only detail on specific consumer round-up or fintech contexts
Much of the underlying evidence base is still retirement-plan literature
packets.relevance_reason: A comprehensive review of behavioural household finance interventions including defaults and choice architecture, giving the effect-size synthesis the brief explicitly wants.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: A randomized reminder nudge cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%; users with an overdraft history saw a net 5% increase in total fees while other users saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil randomizing payment reminders; abstract gives effect sizes on fee outcomes.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows a behavioral nudge that looks beneficial on average can net-harm the exact vulnerable subgroup (those already prone to overdraft/liquidity strain) the support team worries about with passive enrolment, arguing the team should measure subgroup-level harm, not just aggregate enrolment, before defaulting everyone into round-ups.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment defaults
Brazilian credit-card and overdraft context differs from an EU round-up savings pot
no data on persistence beyond the experiment window
packets.relevance_reason: Directly evidences the brief's distributional/manipulation-risk question (C5): a nudge helpful on average can systematically harm a subgroup, the failure mode the brief explicitly wants to avoid building.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: Introduces and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' — a forced-choice design that highlights the losses of the non-preferred option — as a way to nudge behaviour without a default, proposed as a complement or substitute when automatic enrolment is infeasible or ethically fraught.
alternates.methodology: Review of prior active-choice applications (including savings) plus original studies including two field experiments testing standard and enhanced active choice.
alternates.why_it_matters: This is the specific mechanism the brief's active-choice question is asking about: the abstract explicitly frames active choice as an alternative to automatic (opt-out) enrolment for savings behaviour, and the 'enhanced' variant it proposes is a concrete design the round-up feature could adopt to get enrolment lift without full opt-out.
limitations: Field experiments reported are in a healthcare/medication-adherence context, not financial products
No amount-saved or multi-month persistence data reported
No direct comparison to opt-out enrolment on the same population
alternates.relevance_reason: The abstract explicitly names active choice as a savings-behaviour alternative to automatic enrolment and tests an enhanced version of it, which is the specific technique the brief's active-choice decision needs evidence on.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: EU dark-pattern law is best understood as protecting consumer autonomy, and the article develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations for assessing choice-architecture practices like pre-selected defaults.
alternates.methodology: Legal/doctrinal analysis mapping EU consumer-protection law; abstract-only, no empirical measurement.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU legal taxonomy for judging whether an opt-out default or pre-set multiplier reads as manipulative, directly informing how to keep the entry design on the right side of dark-pattern regulation.
limitations: doctrinal/legal analysis, not empirical evidence of behavioral effect
no data on enrolment or savings outcomes
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the brief's EU dark-pattern/manipulation-risk concern for whatever entry design is chosen.
alternates.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
alternates.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

alternates.key_finding: Using 41 million observations on Danish savers, each $1 of subsidy spending (an active-choice-driven policy) raised total saving by only 1 cent, while automatic employer contributions (a default) substantially raised wealth accumulation, because 85% of savers are 'passive' and unresponsive to active-choice incentives.
alternates.methodology: Population-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish retirement savings, decomposing responses to active (subsidy) versus passive (automatic contribution) policy changes.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the argument that active choice captures most of the benefit of a default: shows the large majority of people simply do not respond to an active-choice mechanism, while automatic/default contributions move nearly everyone, a strong quantitative counterweight for the entry-mechanism decision.
limitations: Danish retirement/tax-advantaged savings accounts, not a liquid consumer round-up product
Automatic contributions here are employer-administered, the intermediary mechanism the brief says doesn't transfer
No engagement, withdrawal, or complaint data for the passively-enrolled group
alternates.relevance_reason: The strongest quantitative evidence available on active-choice versus default policy effectiveness, directly bearing on whether active choice can substitute for opt-out, though in a retirement-account setting.
alternates.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
alternates.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

alternates.key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, only 25% of employees opted out within 12 months (versus roughly 50% opt-out at lower defaults per prior literature), and non-opters ended up at a suboptimal contribution level anchored to the default.
alternates.methodology: Observational analysis of a single employer retirement plan's administrative records, compared against a literature review of lower-default plans.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows a preset level can anchor people at a suboptimal rate rather than what they would otherwise choose, directly bearing on the risk of pre-selecting a round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
matched-contribution incentive structure doesn't apply to round-up savings
alternates.relevance_reason: Strong anchoring evidence for the preset-multiplier decision, by analogy from the closest adjacent literature.
alternates.title: Automatic Enrollment with a 12% Default Contribution Rate
alternates.abstract: We study a retirement savings plan with a default contribution rate of 12% of income, which is much higher than previously studied defaults. Twenty-five percent of employees had not opted out of this default 12 months after hire; a literature review finds that the corresponding fraction in plans with lower defaults is approximately one-half. Because only contributions above 12% were matched by the employer, 12% was likely to be a suboptimal contribution rate for employees. Employees who remained at the 12% default contribution rate had average income that was approximately one-third lower than would be predicted from the relationship between salaries and contribution rates among employees who were not at 12%. Defaults may influence low-income employees more strongly in part because these employees face higher psychological barriers to active decision making. Contributions: conceptualized paper (JB, DL, BM, JC), wrote paper (JB, JC), edited paper (DL), implemented empirical analysis (JB, RG), project leadership (JB, JC). The research reported herein was supported by the U.S. Social Security Administration (SSA) through grant #10-M-98363-1-02 to the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) as part of the Retirement Research Consortium (RRC). The findings and conclusions expressed are solely those of the authors and do not represent the views of SSA, any agency of the Federal Government, the RRC, the authors’ universities, or NBER. The authors thank Joshua Rauh and two anonymous reviewers for their comments and thank Yeguang Chi and Richard Lombardo for excellent research assistance. The authors also acknowledge individual and collective financial support from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-AG021650 and T32-AG-000186) and the Pershing Square Fund for Research on the Foundations of Human Behavior.

alternates.key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, are attenuated by 36 months, with modest average savings increases though inequality in savings falls; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
alternates.methodology: Panel data from over 100 US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete medium-run (36-month) horizon on default persistence and separates the enrollment effect from the amount-saved effect and distributional (inequality) effect — precisely the three questions the brief poses, even though the setting is pensions.
limitations: retirement savings, not liquid consumer savings
employer/national pension systems, not a fintech app
structural model's switching-cost estimate may not transfer to a low-friction app setting
alternates.relevance_reason: Recent, methodologically strong evidence separating short vs medium-run default persistence and distributional effects, directly answering the brief's persistence question by analogy.
alternates.title: Default Options and Retirement Saving Dynamics
alternates.abstract: Using data from over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, I document the impact of auto-enrollment (AE) on retirement savings at different horizons. I replicate the impact of AE on participation and contributions in the short run (at 12 months), but I show that these gains are attenuated over the medium run (at 36 months). At this longer horizon, the average savings increases are modest, though AE significantly lowers inequality in savings. To assess AE’s lifetime impact, I estimate a life cycle consumption-savings model that can fit the observed patterns with a switching cost of approximately $250, smaller than previous estimates. (JEL D15, G51, J26, J32)
